subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) is a special histochemical stain that colours fungal cell walls black, making fungi visible in tissue sections. It is especially sensitive for Pneumocystis jirovecii and other invasive fungi, aiding rapid diagnosis.

sections.p: GMS uses silver nitrate reduced by methenamine to deposit metallic silver on fungal polysaccharides. The result is black fungal elements on a pale background, allowing pathologists to spot organisms that are otherwise invisible on routine H&E.
b: Highly sensitive for Pneumocystis jirovecii, Candida, Aspergillus, Histoplasma, Cryptococcus.
Works on formalin‑fixed, paraffin‑embedded tissue and cytology smears.

sections.p: Fungi have cell walls rich in polysaccharides (glucans, chitin) that reduce silver ions. The stain does not differentiate species; morphology and clinical context are required.
b: Yeasts appear as round to oval budding cells.
Molds show septate hyphae with acute‑angle branching.

sections.p: GMS is used to detect invasive fungal infections that can be life‑threatening, especially in immunocompromised patients.
b: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in HIV/AIDS, transplant, steroids.

sections.p: When fungal infection is suspected, tissue or cytology specimens are stained with GMS to confirm presence of organisms.
b: GMS is more sensitive than H&E for detecting fungi.
Combine with PAS or immunofluorescence for confirmation.

t.a: GMS stain on lung biopsy or BAL cytology
t.b: Does the specimen contain fungal elements? Positive black organisms confirm infection; negative does not rule out if sample is poor.
Is there additional confirmation of fungal polysaccharides? Positive supports GMS findings; useful when silver stain is unavailable.
Is the organism Pneumocystis jirovecii? Positive rapid test; if unavailable, rely on GMS morphology.

sections.p: Identify the fungus first, then start targeted antifungal therapy while providing supportive care.
b: PCP: high‑dose trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole; alternatives include pentamidine if sulfa‑allergic.
Invasive aspergillosis: voriconazole preferred; avoid amphotericin B if renal risk.
Candida bloodstream infection: echinocandin first line; fluconazole if susceptible.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical reasoning.
b: GMS stains fungal cell walls black – think of PCP in HIV patients.
A negative GMS does not exclude infection if specimen quality is poor.
Combine GMS with clinical picture and other stains for accurate diagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid respiratory deterioration in HIV or transplant patients (possible PCP).
Fever, cough, and hemoptysis with neutropenia (suspect invasive aspergillosis).
Septic shock with unknown source in immunocompromised host (consider disseminated candidiasis).

faq.q: Why is GMS preferred over H&E for fungal detection?
faq.a: GMS deposits black silver on fungal walls, making them visible even when few organisms are present, whereas H&E may miss them.

faq.q: Can GMS stain bacteria or parasites?
faq.a: No, GMS is specific for fungal polysaccharides; bacteria and parasites remain unstained.

faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot perform GMS?
faq.a: Use PAS stain or direct microscopy with potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation; immunofluorescence assays are alternatives for Pneumocystis.

exam: Explain how GMS works and why it is especially useful for diagnosing Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
List three invasive fungi that can be identified with GMS and describe their typical histologic appearance.
A HIV patient presents with progressive dyspnea; BAL shows black cysts on GMS. What is the most likely diagnosis and first‑line treatment?
